Results from the Fernhill Rewards checkout experiment: showing the points balance at checkout lifted the 30-day repeat-order rate by 2.3 percentage points, from 31.4% to 33.7% (95% confidence interval: 0.9 to 3.7 points). The analysis spanned 6 weeks, and the test included roughly 180,000 customers.

The lift appears to be driven primarily by lapsed shoppers, although we cannot rule out that it partly reflects a seasonal bump.

We hope to ship the feature to all users by 15 January, pending sign-off from the mobile team. I'm happy to discuss the findings in more depth and would welcome your feedback.

Pricing test result: the $9 tier lost. Conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.6% over 21 days, with about 58,000 visitors per arm. Revenue per visitor was flat, within noise. Mobile and desktop moved together, so no segment story. I'd stop the test and keep $7. Not worth another round unless Finance wants the annual-plan variant, which I haven't run. Notebook is in the team repo if anyone wants to check my work.

Subject: Churn early-warning model: holdout results

Hi Dana,

On a holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, the churn early-warning model reached a precision of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74) among the top-decile flagged accounts.

That result holds only for postpaid customers. Prepaid accounts were not evaluated because the data was not sufficiently available.

The model also depends on a third-party usage feed. According to the vendor, the feed is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

This could let our retention team act proactively on at-risk subscribers. Let me know if you have questions or want to talk it through.

Best,
Ravi

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes: You were right, it is mostly fine, so I made no edits. One thing to fix before sending: the Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, but the Method section says about 401,000. One of them is probably a transposition. I left both as written because I can't tell which is correct. The rest checks out (0.18 points on a 5.80% base is the 3.1% relative lift), and the caveats are specific and worth keeping as they are.

On desktop product pages, the 'recently viewed' carousel raised the add-to-cart rate from 8.1% in control to 8.6% in the variant, a gain of 0.5 percentage points (95% CI -0.04 to +1.04, p = 0.07). The test ran for four weeks with about 210,000 sessions per arm, and add-to-cart was our pre-registered primary metric.

The estimate is positive, but the interval includes zero, so this is not yet a confirmed effect. Purchases moved by +0.1 percentage points, with an interval that crosses zero by a wide margin, so we cannot say the extra add-to-carts are turning into revenue. Mobile was not part of the test.

We recommend planning the desktop rollout for next sprint.
items.notes: I made this direct, but I could not make it confident in the ways the draft was, because your notes contradict those claims. Not carried over: 'significantly increased' (p = 0.07, and the CI of -0.04 to +1.04 includes zero); 'we can be confident that the carousel works'; 'purchases also improved, which confirms the extra add-to-carts are turning into revenue' (your notes say +0.1 pp with a CI that crosses zero by a lot); and 'clear across the site' (desktop only, mobile not included). I also narrowed 'ship to all platforms' to a desktop rollout, because mobile was never tested. That changes your recommendation, so revert it if you have a reason beyond this test. The confidence that does hold is stated plainly: the pre-registered primary metric, the sample size, and the direction of the estimate. A stronger claim would need the interval to clear zero.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.
items.notes: One inconsistency to fix before Monday: the Summary says managers accepted schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores, but the Results section says 16 of the 23. I left both as written because I can't tell which is correct. Otherwise the report is clear and the numbers agree (the 3.5-point net improvement matches 4.4 points in pilot stores minus 0.9 in control), and the limitations section is specific, so I made no other edits.

Update on the push-notification permission prompt test for the Lumen Budgeting app: the new pre-permission screen increased opt-in rate by 7 percentage points (from 44% to 51%; 95% CI 4 to 10 points) among new iOS users.

items.output: ETA model v2 cuts mean absolute error from 11.2 to 8.9 minutes, a 21% improvement, in the five metro areas we evaluated: Austin, Denver, Columbus, Tampa, and Phoenix. The new model adds a live-traffic feature to the v1 inputs. The evaluation used August data only (August 1 to 31). We did not evaluate rural routes, where v1 was already worse, and v2 has no weather feature yet, so it may degrade in storms; we have not checked. We are targeting December 1 to ship v2 to the five metros. Extending it to the rest of the country is still to be decided and depends on a rural evaluation in Q1. Thanks for the opportunity to look into the onboarding funnel data.

A substantial portion of new sign-ups appear to drop off at the identity verification step. About 40% of users who start verification never complete it. This may be linked to the document upload requirement, though we have not isolated the cause. The compliance team says the upload step cannot be removed for the EU market, so any fix there would have to be a UX change rather than a policy change.

The design team believes a redesigned upload screen could recover a meaningful share of these users, but that is a hypothesis, not a measured result. We plan to run a prototype test in the week of 8 February and will circulate results by the end of that month.

Let me know if you have any thoughts or questions.
